boundary_note: Bounded first pass for the frozen Fort Blakely record (April 2-9, 1865) in the Mobile Campaign [March-April 1865]. Steele's march from Pensacola, the Spanish Fort record (AL005), the reduction of Batteries Huger and Tracy and the occupation of Mobile are context or separate records. Campaign-wide marches, returns, prisoner totals and multi-action loss totals are context; they are not assigned to one record or added across records. Draft claims do not alter model inputs.

claims.rationale: No inspected return establishes matched personnel at a common opening boundary. The frozen side-specific numerical strength bounds are blank (missing_numeric_strength). No figure in this pass is adopted as a simultaneous opening force.

claims.value: The frozen force field reads XIII and XVI Corps and Fort Blakely Garrison; the live field reads 20,000 (US 16,000; CS 4,000) and NPS says Liddell held with about 4,000 men against 16,000 concentrated for the assault. Andrews says the garrison of Cockrell's (French's) division and Thomas's Alabama reserves numbered about 3,500, and that thirty-five regiments, fully 16,000 troops, took part in the assault, with fifteen or twenty thousand more come up from Spanish Fort in camp two miles back. Canby gives Steele's Pensacola column as 13,200 in mid-March.
claims.rationale: A summary's figures and a participant history's figures for the garrison and the assaulting force, and a mid-March column figure; no matched return. None is adopted as a matched opening strength.

Andrews commanded one of the assaulting divisions. The frozen commanders are Major General John R. Liddell and Major General E. R. S. Canby; the live page gives both as Brigadier General.
claims.rationale: Command roles from the Union commander and an interested participant history; no automatic sole credit, and live ranks are not adopted.

claims.value: The frozen casualty text reads Total 4,475, April 9 only 3,529 (US 629; CS 2,900), and the frozen side rows give 798 US and 3,677 CS; the live field reads 4,475 (US 775; CS 3,700). Canby reports 3,700 prisoners, three of them generals; the Blakely block of his comparative statement is garbled in OCR and ends with the figures 116, 655 and 4, whose columns are not verified. Andrews gives the assaulting troops' loss as 127 killed and 527 wounded, 654 in all, and 3,423 prisoners, and guesses the garrison's killed and wounded at about a third of the besiegers'.
claims.rationale: Original casualty returns were not inspected; preserve totals, categories, cutoffs and differences. No canonical reconciliation or casualty-based opening count; related actions must not be added without resolving population overlap.

open_questions: Liddell's and Cockrell's reports (not printed in the inspected report list), Andrews's report (No. 27), Hawkins's, Pile's, Garrard's and Steele's reports, Andrews's Chapters XXI-XXII on the siege, and the Blakely garrison returns remain deferred.

The organization and casualty returns (Nos. 2-3), the revised casualty statement on p.115, McAlester's engineer report, Granger's, A. J. Smith's, Steele's and the division and brigade reports, Maury's reports and the naval reports remain deferred.

NPS/CWSAC is one family (the NPS battle page plus the frozen Arnold rows). Canby's June 7, 1865 report and the comparative casualty statement printed with it (Official Records Series I, Volume XLIX, Part 1, No. 1) are one family of interested Union accounts. The Official Records volume is a shared container, not an additional witness. Report dates are not event times or proof of contemporary knowledge. C. C. Andrews's History of the Campaign of Mobile (Van Nostrand, 1867) is a retrospective history by the commander of the Second Division, Thirteenth Corps, which took part in the assault; it quotes Liddell's dispatches and Pile's report and shares the Union chain of command with Canby, so it is not independent of the Canby family.
No automatic commander attribution, causal campaign score, morale/readiness number or battle/campaign double counting.
